baseline.selection_reason: Newest longterm (LTS) series at project start; mature Rust-for-Linux support; years of upstream maintenance remaining. See docs/ferret/DECISIONS.md D-001.

components.title: CRC-16 (poly 0x8005, reflected)

symbols.name: crc16
symbols.signature: u16 crc16(u16 crc, const u8 *p, size_t len)

risks: Rust variant is built-in only (CONFIG_CRC16_RUST depends on CRC16=y); loadable-module CRC16 remains the C implementation.
Kernel Rust panics abort the kernel; the implementation has no panic path by construction (256-entry table indexed by u8).
Performance: table-driven byte loop is algorithmically identical to C; measured under QEMU TCG only.
unsafe_boundaries: extern "C" ABI boundary: raw *const u8 with a caller-provided length (same contract as the C original). No other unsafe code.

remaining_c_dependencies.reason: ksymtab entry only, to preserve non-GPL EXPORT_SYMBOL visibility (see DECISIONS D-004)

components.title: CRC-CCITT (poly 0x1021)

symbols.name: crc_ccitt
symbols.signature: u16 crc_ccitt(u16 crc, const u8 *buffer, size_t len)

inline_users: crc_ccitt_byte() remains a static inline in the header and indexes the exported crc_ccitt_table[]; the table is part of the ABI

risks: The exported data table is generated by a const fn at compile time; the differential suite compares all 256 entries against the original C table.
Rust variant is built-in only. CRC_CCITT has no Kconfig prompt, so CRC_CCITT_RUST selects it to force =y; a modular C CRC_CCITT is replaced only by a built-in Rust object.
Kernel Rust panics abort the kernel; the exported function uses unchecked table indexing after a 0xff mask, so it has no bounds-check panic path.
Performance: table-driven byte loop is algorithmically identical to C; measured under QEMU TCG only (not a throughput measurement).
unsafe_boundaries: extern "C" ABI boundary: raw *const u8 with caller-provided length; the pointer is only dereferenced while len > 0.
Table lookup uses get_unchecked with an index masked to 0..=255 (table has 256 entries).

remaining_c_dependencies.reason: ksymtab entries only for crc_ccitt and crc_ccitt_table, preserving non-GPL EXPORT_SYMBOL visibility (DECISIONS D-004); no algorithm

components.title: Generic kernel FIFO (kfifo)
dependencies: kernel::alloc is not used for the FIFO buffer: the allocation flags are a run-time value, so kmalloc_array() is reached through a small C helper (rust/helpers/slab.c)
sg_set_buf() is a static inline without a binding; it is reached through rust/helpers/scatterlist.c
copy_from_user()/copy_to_user() come from the existing Rust-for-Linux helper bindings
call_sites: drivers/iio/buffer/kfifo_buf.c (in-tree consumer through the header macros)
risks: Record-mode framing and partial user-copy semantics are the highest-risk areas; both are covered by the differential suite.
The FIFO is lock-free by contract: the locking rules are the caller's, exactly as in the C original.
smp_wmb() is mapped to a release fence, which is at least as strong as the C barrier on every supported architecture.
The Rust text is 34.7 % larger than the C text (+815 bytes in a 57 MB kernel); the cause is the bounds checking and the wider arithmetic, not a different algorithm.
The throughput measurement was taken under QEMU TCG and is therefore a relative figure only; no native measurement exists.
unsafe_boundaries: The exported functions take a raw `struct __kfifo *`; the pointer is dereferenced once, at the entry of each function.
The backing buffer is turned into a byte slice; the length is derived from the FIFO's own mask and element size.
The copy helpers use copy_nonoverlapping() on pointers derived from those validated slices, with the preconditions (offset inside the buffer, length within the buffer) stated in the SAFETY comments.
The record length bytes are read and written with get_unchecked(): the index is masked to the buffer size, so it is always in bounds.
User memory is accessed through the kernel's copy_from_user()/copy_to_user(), which validate the pointer.

remaining_c_dependencies.reason: ksymtab entries only (23 symbols); no algorithm. Exit condition: per-symbol non-GPL EXPORT_SYMBOL support for Rust translation units.

investigation.prerequisites: none: allocation, user copies and scatterlist support exist in the Rust API

components.title: Kernel bitmap (lib/bitmap.c)
dependencies: the kernel crate needs a way to express a run-time GFP mask (kernel::alloc::Flags::from_gfp) and a NUMA node (kernel::alloc::Vec::with_capacity_in); both were added in this checkpoint
components.call_sites: 1191 files in the tree use the bitmap API (drivers/net, drivers/gpu, fs/xfs, drivers/infiniband, drivers/scsi, ...)
risks: The C bitmap API is used by 1191 files, so a behavioural divergence would be widely visible; the upstream kselftest suite (390447 cases) and the differential suite are the mitigation.
The bit numbering, the word size and the tail bits (the bits above the valid range in the last word) are the areas where a divergence would hide; the differential suite compares them explicitly.
The Rust text is 56 % larger than the C text (+2095 bytes in a 57 MB kernel), mostly in the per-bit helpers, which have no unchecked fast path in the C original.

The weight helpers are slower than the C ones (1327 vs 1000 per mille in the in-kernel benchmark): the kernel's alternatives mechanism patches the C hweight64() to the popcount instruction at boot, and that patch cannot be applied to Rust code. The rest of the API is at parity (884 per mille).
The 32-bit word conversions are implemented but only compiled on a 32-bit target, which Ferret does not build or test: NOT TESTED.
unsafe_boundaries: The exported functions take a raw word pointer; the word count is derived from the bit count and every access is inside it.
bitmap_cut() copies with memmove() semantics, so the destination and the source may overlap, as in the C original.
The record helpers (find_next_bit() and friends) reproduce the semantics of the FIND_NEXT_BIT/FIND_NTH_BIT macros, including the treatment of the bits above the valid range.

remaining_c_dependencies.reason: ksymtab entries only (29 symbols, two of them GPL); no algorithm. Exit condition: per-symbol EXPORT_SYMBOL support for Rust translation units upstream.

investigation.verdict: implemented in checkpoint 003, audited in checkpoint 004
investigation.prerequisites: the run-time allocation mask and the node-aware allocation in the kernel crate, both added in this checkpoint

components.title: Out-of-line reference counting helpers (lib/refcount.c)
dependencies: the refcount_t primitive stays in C (include/linux/refcount.h): it is a header type that the C code embeds in its own structures, and its inline operations are what the kernel's own code calls

the kernel crate needed a borrowed view of a C refcount_t (kernel::sync::Refcount::from_ptr), the saturation-aware operations (try_dec_if_one, try_dec_not_one, warn_saturate, set_saturated) and a handle for C-owned objects (kernel::sync::KRef); all were added in this checkpoint
spin_lock_irqsave() and spin_unlock_irqrestore() are macros, so two C helpers were added to the Rust-for-Linux helper set (rust/helpers/spinlock.c)
components.call_sites: the exported helpers are called from the inline operations of the refcount_t primitive, which the whole kernel uses (include/linux/refcount.h); the primitive itself is embedded in struct kref, struct rcu_head, struct device and others
risks: The exported helpers are on the reference-counting hot path of the whole kernel: the C inline operations of the primitive call refcount_warn_saturate() for every saturation event, so the Rust code is now on that path.

The Rust code calls the C atomic primitives through the kernel crate's Atomic wrapper, which is a real function call, where the C inlined them. The semantics are identical (the same atomic_try_cmpxchg_release() primitive), the cost is one call per operation. This is deliberate: re-implementing the ordering in Rust's own atomics would have been a semantic substitution.
The C WARN_ONCE() uses a racy flag and may print the same warning twice; the Rust version uses an atomic compare-and-exchange and prints it exactly once. The message text is unchanged.
The clean 16-step cycle has not been run for this checkpoint yet, so the component is recorded as partial and not migrated.
unsafe_boundaries: The exported functions take the caller's refcount_t pointer; the Rust code borrows it and never frees or reallocates it.
The lock helpers take the caller's lock pointer and leave the lock held on success, exactly as the C original does; the caller is responsible for releasing it.
The decrement-if-not-one helper reproduces the C loop, including the refusal to decrement a count of one and the underflow warning that returns true without decrementing.
kernel::sync::KRef holds a unique borrow of the C object (PhantomData<&'a mut T>) and a raw pointer to the object; the release callback is the one the C code would pass to kref_put().

remaining_c_dependencies.reason: ksymtab entries only (six symbols); no algorithm. Exit condition: per-symbol EXPORT_SYMBOL support for Rust translation units upstream.

Runtime performance of the Rust crc16() has not been measured; no performance claim is made.
